content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper seeks to improve adversarial robustness by encouraging images that are close to each other to have similar representations. The authors do so by applying small random perturbations to images (they call such images perceptually similar) and adding a loss term to the representation layer. The authors then demonstrate that this method provides some improved robustness, but not as much as standard adversarial training. The authors are careful to do various evaluations to try to establish the validity of their results. 

I vote to reject the paper. The key reason is that prior work already uses the same idea that this paper uses, except the prior work has much better results. I am referring in particular to the work of Zhang et. al [1], first published in January 2019, which performs adversarial training on the representation layer. The method of Zhang et. al has far superior results to performing random noise-based training on the representation layer as this paper does.

If the goal is to enforce similarity of representations for all images within an Lp ball, I feel that the better way to do it is to enforce similarity of representations in the worst case (via adversarial training, as in Zhang et. al) as opposed to doing so via random noise augmentation. The intuition for this comes from the setting when we are only focused on the final logits and not the representation layer. In that setting, simply adding random noise to input images during training does not lead to good adversarial robustness, while adversarial training is much more effective at inducing adversarial robustness.

I would also caution the authors against using the term “perceptual prior” when the authors are simply proposing that the representation layer should be similar when the input images are close to each other in some Lp-norm. The term “perceptual prior” hints at something much more general, while I would argue that this work is still investigating an Lp-ball smoothness prior.

I do appreciate the thoroughness of the experiments that the authors performed, including the ablation tests, and I believe the paper was written fairly clearly.

Additional feedback:

- One possible benefit of this method is that it is faster than adversarial training. The authors point out that scaling adversarial training to ImageNet is difficult - if this is the case, could you show that your method still works on ImageNet?
- What do you mean by “over-fitting to adversarial samples” as a primary drawback of adversarial training in the introduction? This was unclear.
- In equation (1), the superscript in f^j_clean is not explained.
- Section 4.1 can perhaps be combined with section 3.1.
- I also want to point out that ALP is a “broken” adversarial defense [2] because it is not robust to stronger attacks. Thus, this calls into question the results of Tables 2 and 3, where ALP still looks like an effective defense. Perhaps you can run PGD with more steps and more restarts (at least to the point where ALP no longer provides as much robustness) in your evaluations.
- As a note, if you do PGD adversarial training on transformed samples (the way you do for random noise samples), you can also get robustness to transformation attacks [3].

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08573
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.10272
[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02779

content.title: Reply to Official Blind Review #2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. We disagree with the reviewer that the proposed method uses the same idea presented in Zhang et al.[1]. The proposed method and Zhang et al.[1] are very different in terms of computational complexity and loss formulation. Unlike Zhang et al.[1], the proposed method aims at improving the adversarial robustness of models without the use of “adversarial samples”. Following are the major differences:

$Computational\ complexity$:
Zhang et al.[1], uses an iterative method to generate adversarial samples during training.
Proposed method improves the model’s robustness without the use of adversarial samples.

$Loss\ formulation$:
Zhang et al.[1]: regularization term (second term in Eq.(3)[1]), minimizes the cross-entropy between softmax output of the network for clean and their adversarial samples. This formulation would not help to improve the model’s robustness when noisy samples are used instead of adversarial samples. This is because the model is already robust to random noise. So softmax output of clean image and their corresponding noisy counterparts are already similar.
Proposed method: In the paper we first demonstrated that although the softmax output of clean and their noisy images are similar, they differ in their feature representation, and this is the motivation behind the proposed regularizer. The proposed regularizer (second term in Eq.(1)) minimizes the Euclidean distance between  logits of clean and their noisy samples.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
The paper proposes a new training objective for increasing robustness against adversarial examples. The objective includes not only the standard cross entropy loss, but also the loss of the model over randomly perturbed inputs, and also includes a term that penalizes $\ell_2$ distance between logits from perturbed images and their clean counterparts. The paper applies this technique to both increase robustness to $\ell_\infty$ adversaries and rotations/translations of the input image.

This paper has major evaluations that make it unfit for publication. In the paper’s comparison with previous baselines, evaluation produces incorrect results. This calls into question the strength (and implementation) of the attack, and therefore the evaluation of the entire proposed work.

Details:

Issue with evaluation: The paper reports, with PGD steps=100 for CIFAR10 in the $\ell_\infty$ $\epsilon = 8/255$ threat model, that the adversarial accuracies for ALP and the Madry et al defense range around ~94-95%. Neither of these are true, e.g. see [1] for ALP (this paper shows that the ALP defense is easily bypassed with just PGD) and [2] for Madry et al (this readme shows that 20 step PGD gives you ~48%).

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.10272
[2] https://github.com/MadryLab/cifar10_challenge#white-box-leaderboard

display_title: Incorrect and wrong observation by the reviewer.

content.title: Incorrect and wrong observation by the reviewer.
content.comment:
We kindly disagree with the incorrect observation of the reviewer. The results reported in the paper  are in line with the existing work [1]. Unfortunately, the reviewer has  overlooked the captions of tables, while making the remark. This has led the reviewer to assume that all other results reported in the paper are incorrect, leading to an incorrect assessment of the paper. 

In fact, for CIFAR-10, we use PGD attack with steps=20 (please refer to table-2) and not steps=100 (the reviewer might be referring to table-1, but those results are for MNIST dataset, please read the table caption). The accuracies of models trained on CIFAR-10 using PGD adversarial training and ALP are around 43% to 51%, and are not around ~94-95% as observed by the reviewer. The reviewer might be comparing results on MNIST dataset (table-2) to the results of CIFAR-10 dataset provided in [1], which is wrong. 

[1] Madry et al. “Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks” ICLR 2018

replying_to: Replying to Incorrect and wrong observation by the reviewer.

content.title: Point still stands
content.comment:
Thank you for pointing out my mistake. My overall point still stands though: in the evaluation for CIFAR-10, the evaluation indicates that ALP is more robust than PGD adversarial training, which cannot be true as ALP is a broken defense. As further indication that the evaluation is not thorough enough, PGD with 7 steps and PGD with 20 steps give significantly different robustness values (for both ALP and the proposed defense). 

In order to show that the defense is truly robust, the authors must use more steps in their evaluation; currently the attack is not strong enough to break ALP, a broken defense.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper proposes a regularizer on logit similarity to improve model robustness to adversarial examples. 

The introduction needs a bit of work to separate the context of the present submission, the submission’s contributions, and the related work. There is also some overlap with content presented in Section 2. Some of the terminology could also be improved to remove ambiguity in the writing. For instance, adversarial examples are not constructed using “noise”. Because noise is used in Section 2 to refer to adversarial perturbations, it is not clear from the current write up whether later uses of the term “noise”, e.g., in Section 3, refer to an adversarial perturbation or random noise. 

Robustness claims are backed up by empirical validation, however the experimental setup falls short to provide sufficient evidence. To help the authors assess what evidence is sufficient, I would recommend consulting [https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06705], which provides guidelines for the proper evaluation of robustness to adversarial examples. The report is more comprehensive, but some of the aspects that need to be improved include in particular:

* The attack does not use sufficiently enough PGD iterations. 
* Transferability experiments are mounted with the FGSM only. 
* It is possible that the similarity between logits is a good regularizer against attacks that only target the final prediction of the model (i.e., the output of the softmax) but not adaptive attacks. One such possible attack would have the adversary generate an input that targets earlier layers of the model rather than the softmax. Considering such adaptive attacks would also contribute to strengthening the evaluation of robustness claims made here.

Another point of comparison that is missing from the evaluation are verifiable training procedures. For instance, PixelDP [https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03471] and smoothing [https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02918] would be good baselines to add to the experiments, at least for datasets where results are available (e.g., MNIST and CIFAR10). None of the approaches used in the evaluation are certifiable. 

Nitpick on page 7: Gradient masking was introduced in [https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.02697] prior to Athalye et al.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer-1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. In Sec.4.4 of the paper, we have provided the results for the important sanity tests which are described in [1]. We perform PGD attack with a large number of steps on WRN-28-10 trained using the proposed method. Table below shows the obtained results. It can be observed the model’s accuracy does not degrade significantly with increase in the number of steps.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
|        WRN-28-10 trained on CIFAR-10                    |
+----------+-----------------------------------------------------+
|                    |            PGD attack                               |  
|                    +--------------+----------+----------+---------+
|                    | steps=50  |    100   |  500     | 1000  |
+---------------+--------------+----------+---------+-----------+
| Proposed |       27.64   | 27.43  | 27.36  | 27.35   |
+---------------+--------------+----------+---------+-----------+

Further, we will include the suggestion to improve the paper.
[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.00420
